title: Imam al-Maturidi
hookLine: a theologian in Samarqand, close to the Ash'aris, with one difference worth knowing

cards: All week the stage has been Basra and Baghdad. Now go east, past Iran, across the great river, into what is now Uzbekistan. Samarqand: a city of traders and scholars on the Silk Road.
A theologian named Abu Mansur al-Maturidi taught there; his name, the sources say, comes from Maturid, a quarter of the city.
He was a Hanafi, trained in the legal school of Abu Hanifa, and he wrote a book called simply Kitab al-Tawhid, the book of oneness.
He worked on the same questions as al-Ash'ari, far from Basra, and reached answers that sit very close.

teach.b: Start with how close the two schools are. Ash'aris and Maturidis both defend traditional Sunni belief with reason. Both say the Qur'an is Allah's uncreated speech, and both affirm His attributes.
Later scholars often named them together as the two Sunni schools of kalam, and the Maturidi school became tied especially with Hanafi scholars. Now the one difference worth learning.

teach.h: CAN REASON KNOW GOOD AND BAD?
teach.b: Can a person know by reason alone that some things are good and some are bad, before any messenger arrives? The Ash'aris said our obligations come from revelation: without a messenger, no duty is laid on us.
Al-Maturidi gave reason a bigger job. Reason, in his view, can recognize that lying is ugly and that gratitude is right, and can even grasp that the world has a Maker who deserves thanks.

Revelation confirms and fills in what reason sees; it doesn't contradict it. Both schools agree that Allah is just and that the Qur'an guides. They disagree about how much the mind can see on its own.
That's a fair disagreement, and Sunni scholars kept both schools in their curricula.

And that rounds off a week: faith that rises and falls, kalam, the Mu'tazilah and their justice, the trial and Ahmad ibn Hanbal's refusal, al-Ash'ari's turn, his school's middle way, and now Samarqand.
One conversation, carried from city to city.

how: The Maturidi school is studied alongside the Ash'ari school in Sunni seminaries, and it is followed especially by Hanafi scholars.

o: a Hanafi judge of Baghdad who ran the caliph's test of scholars
a Mu'tazili thinker of Basra who said the Qur'an was created
a Hanafi theologian of Samarqand who gave reason a larger role

p: can see some good and bad, he said

s: he defended traditional Sunni belief, very close to the Ash'aris.
Maturidis say reason can recognize some things as good or bad
revelation confirms and fills in what reason sees.
Ash'aris and Maturidis disagree on whether the Qur'an is created
both say it is Allah's uncreated speech.

games.q: before any messenger arrives, can a person know by reason that gratitude is right?
o: al-Maturidi: yes, reason can see some good and bad.
nobody in Islamic theology ever asked this.
both schools said exactly the same thing.
games.why: al-Maturidi gave reason a bigger role; the Ash'aris tied obligation to revelation. Both say Allah is just.

practice: Think of one thing you know is good without looking it up: thanking someone who helped you, or telling the truth when a lie would be easier.
Ask the Samarqand question, how do I know this is good, from a text, from a parent, or from something in me that recognizes it, and just notice where the knowing seems to come from.
If you pray, you can give thanks for whatever showed it to you.

wordCard.voice: Imam al-Maturidi. The Hanafi theologian of Samarqand, close to the Ash'aris, who gave reason a larger role in knowing good and bad. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: the Maturidi, after Maturid, a neighborhood of Samarqand.

carryVoice: Your line: from samarqand. The same questions, asked far to the east. That's a week of the theologians.
